title: Arjuna sees only the bird
hookLine: Drona asks his students what they see, and only Arjuna sees nothing but the bird
carry: samadhi: the mind gathered on one seed
tomorrow: what brings you near, if not talent?
last: ABHYASA AND VAIRAGYA: PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.

lines: A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.
cards: The Mahabharata. Drona, teacher of the young princes, has a wooden bird set high in a tree, then calls his students one at a time. Aim at the bird, he says, and tell me what you see.
Yudhishthira, the eldest, says: the tree, the bird, you, my brothers. Step aside, says Drona. Brother after brother gives the same kind of answer.

teach.h: ONLY THE BIRD. ONLY ITS HEAD.
teach.b: What do you see? Only the bird. Not the tree, not you.
Describe the bird, says Drona. I see only its head. Shoot, says Drona, and Arjuna's arrow takes the head off the bird.
Popular retellings make it the bird's eye; either way, everything else has fallen away.
Patanjali's school has a word for a mind gathered like that: ekagra, one-pointed, and the commentator Vyasa says that's the kind of mind in which samadhi happens.
Samadhi means absorption, the mind so gathered that the scattering stops.
Sutra 1.17 describes the first kind, absorption with an object, in four stages from coarse to fine: something physical, then something subtle, then joy, then the bare sense of I am.
In every stage the mind still rests on something, a support. Later in the chapter Patanjali calls this samadhi with seed, sabija.
Sutra 1.18 describes the other kind: practice lets go of even the support, and only faint traces, the samskaras, remain. No object at all. That's the far end.

teach.h: A NAME, A FLAME, ONE SEED.
teach.b: But nearly every Hindu who meditates starts with a seed: a mantra, a name of God, a lamp's flame, the face of God on the home altar, the breath.
It's why so much Hindu prayer is repetition and gazing: the same name a hundred and eight times, the same murti every evening at aarti. One bird. Everything else falls away.
So the week ran from bhakti, through tat tvam asi, into a new book: now, the seer, the five turnings, practice and letting go, and today, one seed.

how: Teachers of classical yoga describe samadhi in stages, first with an object of meditation and then beyond any object, and students usually work for years with a single support, such as the breath, a mantra or a divine form.

o: a deep sleep in which the mind drifts away
with seed: absorption that still rests on something
a seed mantra given by a teacher at initiation

games.q: the stages of samadhi with seed.
p: absorbed in the bare sense of I am

s: Patanjali describes only one kind of samadhi
1.17 gives samadhi with an object, in four stages; 1.18 gives the kind with no object.
in the Mahabharata, Arjuna tells Drona he sees only the bird
then only its head. the others saw the tree, the teacher and their brothers too.
samadhi without seed leaves only faint impressions

games.q: you're absorbed so deeply in a name of God that nothing else exists. which samadhi is this, in Patanjali's terms?
o: samadhi with seed: the name is still a support.
samadhi without seed: nothing is held.
games.why: as long as the mind rests on something, a name, a flame, even the breath, it's samadhi with an object, with seed. Arjuna's bird, not yet the empty sky.

practice: Give the mind one seed. If you pray, light a diya or a candle before an image of God that's yours, or hold one name; if you don't, use a candle flame or one small object.
Rest your eyes and attention on it, the way Arjuna saw only the bird. When the tree and the brothers creep back in, other sounds, plans, thoughts, let them go and come back to the one thing.
If even the seed thins out for a moment, let it, without chasing it.

wordCard.voice: Sabija, with seed. Samadhi that still rests on a support, coarse or subtle, joy or the bare sense of I am, as opposed to absorption with no seed at all.

orig.note: Sanskrit samādhi: absorption, the mind fully gathered; literally a putting-together.

carryVoice: Your line: samadhi, the mind gathered on one seed. Only the bird. Week sixty-two, done.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras of Patanjali 1.17–1.18 (samprajnata and the other samadhi)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Drona tests his pupils with a bird on a tree; Arjuna sees only its head)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 1.1 (the one-pointed mind, ekagra, and samprajnata samadhi)
